questions.title: Circular motion of a clock's minute hand — angular speed, distance & centripetal acceleration

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
The minute hand completes one revolution in 1 hour, so T = 60 × 60 s.
ω = 2π/T = 2π/(60 × 60) = 1.7 × 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: L = arc length/angle = 0.44/2.4 = 0.18 m

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer: The centripetal acceleration (5.5 × 10⁻⁷ m s⁻²) is negligible compared with the acceleration of free fall (9.81 m s⁻²), so the resultant force on the clay is negligible compared with its weight. The force exerted by the minute hand therefore remains approximately equal (and opposite) to the weight throughout the revolution, so its variation is negligible.

questions.title: Gravitational potential & escape speed — the Moon's field & hydrogen atmosphere

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: E_P = mφ (the gravitational potential energy is the mass multiplied by the gravitational potential at its position).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
At escape the total energy of the particle is zero: ½mv² + mφ = 0.
½v² = −φ, so v² = −2φ and v = √(−2φ)

parts.label: (e)
parts.answer: The r.m.s. speed is only an average, so there is a distribution of molecular speeds and many hydrogen molecules have speeds greater than the escape speed (2400 m s⁻¹). These molecules escape, so the Moon does not retain a hydrogen atmosphere.

questions.title: Internal energy & the first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of the molecules/particles of the system — the total energy of their random motion.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: No thermal energy is transferred (q = 0). Work is done <u>on</u> the spring, which increases the potential energy of its particles, so from ΔU = q + W the internal energy increases.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Thermal energy is transferred <u>to</u> the water (q > 0), while the water does work against the atmosphere as it vaporises (W < 0). More thermal energy is transferred in than the work done out, so the internal energy increases.

questions.title: Coulomb's law — charged oil droplet in equilibrium between plates

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The electric force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Negative — the electric force must act upwards to balance the weight, i.e. opposite to the direction of the field.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: Four equally spaced straight field lines perpendicular to the plates, running from the top plate to the bottom plate, with arrows pointing downwards.

questions.title: Capacitor discharge — energy stored, capacitance & time constant

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Energy stored = area under the V–Q graph = ½QV = ½ × 450 × 10⁻⁶ × 8.0 = 1.8 × 10⁻³ J = 1.8 mJ

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC) with τ = RC. At one time constant t = τ: V/8.0 = e⁻¹, so ln(V/8.0) = −1.0, i.e. −ln(V/8.0) = 1.0.

questions.title: Photoelectric effect — photon energy, Planck constant & work function

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: A photon is a quantum (packet) of electromagnetic radiation energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Photoelectric effect (photoelectric emission).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: An electron needs a minimum energy to escape from the metal, and this energy must be absorbed as a single whole packet (photon) whose energy depends on frequency. The intensity of the radiation determines only the number of photons, not the energy of each, so below the threshold frequency no electron can escape however intense the radiation — evidence that the energy is quantised.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Planck constant (h) — the gradient of the E_k,max against f graph.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: −(the) work function (energy) — the y-intercept of the extrapolated line.

questions.title: Fluorine-18 PET scanning — tracer decay, annihilation & gamma-ray imaging

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: A tracer is a substance containing radioactive nuclei that is introduced into the body and absorbed by the tissue being studied, so that its position can be detected.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: X = β⁺ (a positron, e⁺); P = 1; Q = 0; R = 18.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The positrons emitted in the decay annihilate with electrons in the tissue; the mass of the particles is converted into the energy of a pair of gamma-ray photons travelling in opposite directions, which leave the body.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: The arrival times of the gamma-ray photons at the detectors are processed to build up an image of the concentration of the tracer in the tissue.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: A = λN and λ = ln 2/T, with N = n × N_A. Two photons are produced from each decay, so R₀ = 2λnN_A = (2 ln 2) nN_A / T

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: Sketch an exponential decay curve from (0, R₀), passing through (T, R₀/2) and (2T, R₀/4), with a negative gradient of continuously decreasing magnitude.

questions.title: Wien's law, standard candle & redshift corrections

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Wien's displacement law: the wavelength λ_max at which the rate of emission of radiation from the surface is a maximum is inversely proportional to the thermodynamic (surface) temperature T, i.e. λ_max ∝ 1/T.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: A standard candle is an (astronomical) object of known luminosity.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: The star (and its galaxy) is moving away from the observer, so the received wavelengths are increased (redshifted).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: wavelength of radiation: too high (redshifted); surface temperature: too low (Wien: T ∝ 1/λ, and λ is overestimated); distance to star: unchanged (the standard candle gives the true distance); radius of star: too high (Stefan–Boltzmann: with T underestimated, r is overestimated).
